claim: Zebrafish neurohypophyseal synapses are enriched with multiple large dense core vesicles (LDCV).
source: We observed that neurohypohyseal synapses were enriched with multiple large dense core vesicles (LDCV) (Figure 1B & C).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) observations presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 1B & C.

claim: Neurohypophyseal synapses in zebrafish exhibit exocytosis of LDCV content.
source: We also observed an occurrence of LDVCs content exocytosis, typical of previously reported synaptic neurosecretion in the neurohypophysis (Boudier, 1974; Buma and Nieuwenhuys, 1987; Douglas et al., 1970; Douglas, 1973; Hayashi et al., 1994; Santolaya et al., 1972).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM observations in the manuscript and citations to previous literature on neurohypophyseal neurosecretion.

claim: Neurohypophyseal synapses are located next to the basement membrane of endothelial cells.
source: Neurohypophyseal synapses were located next to the basement membrane of the endothelial cells (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM imaging data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Exocytotic pits with fused LDCV membranes were observed next to the perivascular space in neurohypophyseal synapses.
source: In particular, we observed exocytotic pits, in which the membranes of LDCVs were fused with the plasma membrane, next to the perivascular space (Figure 1B', arrow).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM observations shown in Figure 1B'.

claim: Electron-dense plasma membrane invaginations and recycled vesicles were detected in neurohypophyseal synapses, indicating endocytosis.
source: Moreover, we detected electron-dense plasma membrane invaginations (Figure 1C' red arrowhead) and recycled vesicles in the cytoplasm (Figure 1C', white arrowhead) indicating a membrane retrieval process by endocytosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM observations shown in Figure 1C'.

claim: Coupling of synaptic exocytosis and endocytosis is typical for neuronal synapses and is a general mechanism for conservation of cell surface upon neurosecretion.
source: Coupling of synaptic exocytosis and endocytosis is typical for neuronal synapses and considered as a general mechanism for conservation of the cell surface upon neurosecretion (Damer and Creutz, 1994; De Camilli, 1995; Douglas, 1973; Kononenko and Haucke, 2015; Rizzoli, 2014; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature on synaptic mechanisms.

claim: Almost all neurohypophyseal anti-OXT immunoreactive puncta co-localized with Synaptophysin-EGFP with a mean weighted colocalization coefficient of 0.87.
source: We observed that almost all the neurohypophyseal anti-OXT immunoreactive puncta co-localized with Synaptophysin-EGFP (Mean weighted colocalization coefficient = 0.87, n = 5 larvae), indicating that mature OXT neuropeptides are located exclusively within neurohypophyseal synaptic axonal swellings (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis of immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mature OXT neuropeptides are located exclusively within neurohypophyseal synaptic axonal swellings.
source: We observed that almost all the neurohypophyseal anti-OXT immunoreactive puncta co-localized with Synaptophysin-EGFP (Mean weighted colocalization coefficient = 0.87, n = 5 larvae), indicating that mature OXT neuropeptides are located exclusively within neurohypophyseal synaptic axonal swellings (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the high colocalization coefficient between OXT and synaptic markers.

claim: Hypertonic osmotic challenge induces a robust release of oxytocin and vasopressin and reduced neuropeptide content in the pituitary of both mammals and fish.
source: To validate our detection method, we subjected the fish to hypertonic osmotic challenge (25% sea salt) (Figure 2A), which is known to induce a robust release of oxytocin and vasopressin and, consequently reduced neuropeptide content in the pituitary of both mammals and fish (Balment et al., 1980; Huang et al., 1996; Leng and Russell, 2019; Pierson et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on osmotic challenge effects.

claim: The number of EGFP-positive synapses remained unaltered following acute hypertonic challenge.
source: While the number of these EGFP-positive synapses remained unaltered following acute hypertonic challenge, both the synaptic and OXT puncta volumes were decreased (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of synapses shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Both the synaptic and OXT puncta volumes were decreased following acute hypertonic challenge.
source: While the number of these EGFP-positive synapses remained unaltered following acute hypertonic challenge, both the synaptic and OXT puncta volumes were decreased (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2C and 2E.

claim: Recovery of larvae from hypertonic to isotonic condition for 1 hr led to partial-reversal of the observed phenotypes.
source: Recovery of larvae from hypertonic to isotonic condition (for 1 hr) led to partial-reversal of the observed phenotypes (Figure 2C and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2C and 2E.

claim: The results of hypertonic challenge are in agreement with hypertonicity-induced cell shrinking mechanisms essential for osmosensation in OXT neurons.
source: These results are in agreement with the reported hypertonicity-induced cell shrinking mechanisms essential for osmosensation in these neurons (Prager-Khoutorsky et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on osmosensation mechanisms.

claim: OXT-specific expression of BoTxLCB led to increased volume of OXT puncta without affecting the number and volume of synapses.
source: OXT-specific expression of BoTxLCB led to increased volume of OXT puncta, but without affecting the number and volume of the synapses, indicative of accumulation of OXT content (Figure 2G–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2G-J.

claim: The increased synaptic OXT level in BoTxLCB transgenic larvae under naïve conditions was maintained following hypertonic challenge.
source: The increased synaptic OXT level we observed in BoTxLCB transgenic larvae under naïve conditions, was maintained following hypertonic challenge.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2I-J.

claim: Both basal OXT release and hypertonic osmotic challenge-induced OXT release are blocked by expression of BoTxLCB.
source: These results suggest that both basal OXT release and hypertonic osmotic challenge- induced OXT release are blocked by expression of BoTxLCB.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that OXT levels remain high in BoTxLCB-expressing neurons even after hypertonic challenge.

claim: F-actin regulates multiple aspects of vesicular homeostasis such as presynaptic vesicular capture, clustering, docking, release, recycling and inter-synaptic exchange.
source: Several recent studies reported that F-actin regulates multiple aspects of vesicular homeostasis such as presynaptic vesicular capture, clustering, docking, release, recycling and inter-synaptic exchange (Chia et al., 2014; Ganguly et al., 2015; Guillet et al., 2016; Marra et al., 2012; Miki et al., 2016; Soykan et al., 2017; Stavoe and Colón-Ramos, 2012; Vincent et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on F-actin function in synapses.

claim: Actin is required for recruitment of multiple synaptic proteins and receptors that are essential for synaptic function.
source: Actin is also required for recruitment of multiple synaptic proteins and receptors that are essential for synaptic function (Sankaranarayanan et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on actin function in synapses.

claim: In rat neurohypophyseal synapses, actin filaments are arranged both in the synaptic cytoplasm associated with vesicles and along the plasma membrane.
source: In rat neurohypophyseal synapses, EM studies have shown that actin filaments are arranged both in the synaptic cytoplasm associated with the vesicles and along the plasma membrane (Alonso et al., 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to EM studies in rat neurohypophysis.

claim: Perturbation of isolated neurohypophyseal tissue using actin disrupting agents leads to release of OXT, suggesting that cortical actin is required to prevent release of synaptic OXT.
source: Furthermore, perturbation of isolated neurohypophyseal tissue using actin disrupting agents leads to release of OXT, suggesting that cortical actin is required to prevent release of synaptic OXT (Tobin and Ludwig, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on actin disruption effects.

claim: Lifeact-EGFP signal exhibited a cage-like structure surrounding OXT in neurohypophyseal synapses.
source: Imaging revealed various characteristics of actin and neuropeptides. Lifeact-EGFP signal exhibited a cage-like structure surrounding OXT in neurohypophyseal synapses (Figure 3B–D and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution STORM microscopy data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: The cage-like structure of actin filaments surrounding OXT is in agreement with previous reports that actin filaments form a cage-like structure associated with synaptic vesicles.
source: These results are in agreement with previous reports that actin filaments form a cage-like structure associated with synaptic vesicles (Hirokawa et al., 1989; Miyamoto, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on actin organization in synapses.

claim: Cytochalasin D treatment at 400 nM reduced the number and size of synaptic axonal swellings.
source: Subsequent analysis revealed that the number and size of the synaptic axonal swellings was reduced upon cytochalasin D treatment (Figure 3E,F), which is in agreement with the involvement of F-actin in regulating the synaptic morphology (Zhang and Benson, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Cytochalasin D treatment affected both the number and volume of OXT puncta.
source: Cytochalasin D treatment also affected both the number and volume of OXT puncta (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: Cofilin is a member of ADF family of actin-binding proteins that promote F-actin depolymerizing and regulates its turnover.
source: Cofilin is a member of ADF family of actin-binding proteins that promote F-actin depolymerizing and regulates its turnover (Shekhar and Carlier, 2017; Wioland et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on Cofilin function.

claim: Expression of control EGFP alone did not affect number and volume of OXT puncta.
source: We observed that expression of control EGFP alone did not affect number and volume of OXT puncta however, expression of Cofilin-EGFP led to decreased OXT puncta volume (Figure 3I–N) with a large effect size of Cohen's d of 0.93, p-value<0.05 (Cohen, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3I-K.

claim: Expression of Cofilin-EGFP led to decreased OXT puncta volume with a large effect size of Cohen's d of 0.93, p-value<0.05.
source: We observed that expression of control EGFP alone did not affect number and volume of OXT puncta however, expression of Cofilin-EGFP led to decreased OXT puncta volume (Figure 3I–N) with a large effect size of Cohen's d of 0.93, p-value<0.05 (Cohen, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3L-N.

claim: Actin polymerization regulates synaptic OXT neuropeptide content.
source: Together, the above results suggest that actin polymerization regulates synaptic OXT neuropeptide content.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of cytochalasin D treatment and Cofilin expression experiments.

claim: Robo2 is localized to axonal growth cones and is known to regulate axonal guidance by modulating actin dynamics via other actin interacting regulatory proteins.
source: Robo2 is localized to axonal growth cones and is known to regulate axonal guidance by modulating actin dynamics via other actin interacting regulatory proteins (Kidd et al., 1998; Slováková et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Robo2 function.

claim: robo2 mRNA is expressed in OXT neurons.
source: Fluorescent in situ hybridization of robo2 mRNA showed that it is expressed in OXT neurons (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The recovery of Lifeact-EGFP fluorescence was attenuated in OXT synapses of robo2-/- mutants compared to robo2+/+ zebrafish.
source: Indeed, in comparison to the robo2+/+ zebrafish, the recovery of Lifeact-EGFP fluorescence was attenuated in OXT synapses of robo2-/- mutants (Figure 4D), which exhibited decreased dynamic Lifeact-EGFP fraction and increased stable fraction (Figure 4E,F; Cohen's d effect size 0.67, p value < 0.05.)
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: robo2-/- mutants exhibited decreased dynamic Lifeact-EGFP fraction and increased stable fraction with Cohen's d effect size 0.67, p value < 0.05.
source: Indeed, in comparison to the robo2+/+ zebrafish, the recovery of Lifeact-EGFP fluorescence was attenuated in OXT synapses of robo2-/- mutants (Figure 4D), which exhibited decreased dynamic Lifeact-EGFP fraction and increased stable fraction (Figure 4E,F; Cohen's d effect size 0.67, p value < 0.05.)
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP analysis shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Robo2 signaling regulates synaptic actin dynamics of neurohypophyseal OXT neurons.
source: This suggests that Robo2 signaling regulates synaptic actin dynamics of neurohypophyseal OXT neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the FRAP analysis showing altered actin dynamics in robo2 mutants.

claim: The volume of OXT puncta was smaller in robo2-/- fish compared to WT controls with a large effect size (Cohen's d of 0.82, p value<0.05).
source: We found that the volume of OXT puncta was smaller in robo2-/- fish compared to WT controls with a large effect size (Cohen's d of 0.82, p value<0.05), while the number and size of neurohypophyseal synapses were largely unaffected, suggesting that Robo2 regulates synaptic oxytocin levels without affecting synaptic morphogenesis (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The number and size of neurohypophyseal synapses were largely unaffected in robo2-/- mutants.
source: We found that the volume of OXT puncta was smaller in robo2-/- fish compared to WT controls with a large effect size (Cohen's d of 0.82, p value<0.05), while the number and size of neurohypophyseal synapses were largely unaffected, suggesting that Robo2 regulates synaptic oxytocin levels without affecting synaptic morphogenesis (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Robo2 regulates synaptic oxytocin levels without affecting synaptic morphogenesis.
source: We found that the volume of OXT puncta was smaller in robo2-/- fish compared to WT controls with a large effect size (Cohen's d of 0.82, p value<0.05), while the number and size of neurohypophyseal synapses were largely unaffected, suggesting that Robo2 regulates synaptic oxytocin levels without affecting synaptic morphogenesis (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that OXT content is reduced without changes in synapse number or size.

claim: The phenotype in robo2 mutants was not due to OXT axonal guidance deficits, as the number of neurohypophyseal OXT axonal projections was similar between robo2-/- and robo2+/+ fish larvae.
source: This phenotype was not due to OXT axonal guidance deficits, as the number of neurohypophyseal OXT axonal projections was similar between robo2-/- and robo2+/+ fish larvae (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: slit3 is highly expressed in the developing neurohypophysis.
source: We recently identified that slit3, a cognate ligand for Robo2 is highly expressed in the developing neurohypophysis (Anbalagan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Knock-down of slit3 using morpholino led to reduced synaptic OXT content similar to the robo2 mutant phenotype.
source: Knock-down of slit3 using a previously validated morpholino antisense oligonucleotide targeted to the translational start site (Barresi et al., 2005), led to reduced synaptic OXT content similar to the robo2 mutant phenotype (Figure 5F–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5F-J.

claim: The volume of OXT puncta was significantly reduced following slit3 knockdown compared to mock injected controls (Cohen's d effect size 1.12, p value < 0.01).
source: Thus, the volume of OXT puncta was significantly reduced following slit3 knockdown, compared to mock injected controls (Cohen's d effect size 1.12, p value < 0.01), while the number, size of neurohypophyseal synapses and number of neurohypophyseal OXT axonal projections were unaffected.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The number, size of neurohypophyseal synapses and number of neurohypophyseal OXT axonal projections were unaffected by slit3 knockdown.
source: Thus, the volume of OXT puncta was significantly reduced following slit3 knockdown, compared to mock injected controls (Cohen's d effect size 1.12, p value < 0.01), while the number, size of neurohypophyseal synapses and number of neurohypophyseal OXT axonal projections were unaffected.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5F,G,H,J.

claim: POMC cells are arranged in two clusters, anterior and posterior, abutting neurohypophyseal OXT axons and synapses respectively.
source: To investigate the role of Slit3 locally, we employed the Tg(pomc:Gal4) driver that enabled local secretion of Slit3-EmGFP fusion protein from proopiomelanocortin (POMC) cells that are arranged in two clusters, anterior and posterior, abutting neurohypophyseal OXT axons and synapses respectively (Figure 5K).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Enlarged volume of OXT puncta was detected adjacent to Slit3-EmGFP-positive clones located in a posterior but not anterior position.
source: Interestingly, when comparing to tRFP expressing clones we detected enlarged volume of OXT puncta adjacent to Slit3-EmGFP-positive clones located in a posterior but not anterior position (Figure 5M–R).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5M-R.

claim: The localized effect of Slit3 coincided with the posterior position of the endogenous OXT synapses.
source: As depicted schematically in Figure 5L, this localized effect of Slit3 coincided with the posterior position of the endogenous OXT synapses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the spatial relationship between Slit3 expression and OXT synapse location.

claim: Localized context-dependent Slit3-Robo2 signaling regulates synaptic OXT levels.
source: These results suggest that localized context-dependent Slit3-Robo2 signaling regulates synaptic OXT levels.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the position-dependent effects of Slit3 on OXT content.

claim: The EGFP-tagged OXT transgenic protein product mainly co-localized with the mature (i.e. cleaved and cyclised) endogenous OXT neuropeptide.
source: This revealed that the EGFP-tagged OXT transgenic protein product mainly co-localized with the mature (i.e. cleaved and cyclised) endogenous OXT neuropeptide (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by triple co-immunostaining data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In some cases, the OXT-GFP reporter protein co-localized with vesicles containing both cleaved and OXT-neurophysin protein, suggesting that it reported an intermediate step in the proteolytic processing of the OXT precursor peptide.
source: As expected, in some cases, the OXT-GFP reporter protein co-localized with vesicles containing both cleaved and OXT-neurophysin protein, suggesting that it reported an intermediate step in the proteolytic processing of the OXT precursor peptide (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the colocalization patterns observed in immunostaining.

claim: Similar to the endogenous OXT, the EGFP-OXT reporter exhibited a clustered organization, indicative of large dense core vesicular organization of OXT.
source: Our results showed that similar to the endogenous OXT, the EGFP-OXT reporter exhibited a clustered organization, indicative of large dense core vesicular organization of OXT (Figure 6D,E and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution STORM microscopy data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: mCherry-Utrophin-CH co-localizes with OXT-loaded synaptic vesicles.
source: We expressed mCherry-Utrophin-CH in OXT neurons in combination with our Tg(oxt:oxt-SP-EGFP) that labels OXT-loaded vesicles in synapses and found that mCherry-Utrophin-CH co-localizes with OXT-loaded synaptic vesicles (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: F-actin is enriched near OXT synaptic vesicles.
source: This result further supports our original suggestion that that F-actin is enriched near OXT synaptic vesicles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the colocalization of F-actin probe with OXT vesicles.

claim: Upon bleaching, gradual recovery of EGFP-OXT fluorescence was observed indicating the mobilization of transiting OXT-loaded vesicles in the synapses.
source: Upon bleaching, we observed gradual recovery of EGFP-OXT fluorescence indicating the mobilization of transiting OXT-loaded vesicles in the synapses.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP analysis shown in Figure 6H,I.

claim: The extent of fluorescence recovery was low (13%), suggesting that the majority of the bleached OXT-EGFP-positive vesicles were stationary and not mobile.
source: The extent of fluorescence recovery was low (13%), suggesting that the majority of the bleached OXT-EGFP-positive vesicles were stationary and not mobile (Figure 6H,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP analysis shown in Figure 6H,I.

claim: The fluorescence recovery rate in robo2-/- mutants was significantly lower than in robo2+/+ larvae.
source: FRAP analysis in transgenic larvae on the background of robo2 mutants revealed that the fluorescence recovery rate in robo2-/- mutants, was significantly lower than in robo2+/+ larvae (Figure 6I).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP analysis shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Robo2-mediated signaling regulates actin dynamics as well as the accumulation of OXT-containing vesicles in neurohypophyseal synapses.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Robo2-mediated signaling regulates actin dynamics as well as the accumulation of OXT-containing vesicles in neurohypophyseal synapses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of FRAP analyses of both actin and OXT vesicles.

claim: Robo signaling is known to affect the transition of the Rho-GTPase protein Cdc42 from GTP- to GDP- bound state, resulting in decreased actin polymerization.
source: Robo signaling is known to affect the transition of the Rho-GTPase protein Cdc42 from GTP- to GDP- bound state, resulting in decreased actin polymerization (Wong et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on Robo-Cdc42 signaling.

claim: High EGFP fluorescence led to decreased OXT levels in both robo2+/+ and robo2-/- larvae (p<0.01, adj. R2 = 0.93 and 0.85 respectively).
source: Regression analysis of OXT fluorescence as a function of EGFP fluorescence in each injected zebrafish larvae showed that high EGFP fluorescence led to decreased OXT levels in both robo2+/+ and robo2-/- larvae (Figure 7C; p<0.01, adj. R2 = 0.93 and 0.85 respectively) (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The effect of high EGFP fluorescence on decreased OXT levels is likely due to overexpression of the untethered EGFP.
source: This effect is likely due to overexpression of the untethered EGFP.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of EGFP effect.

claim: Expression levels of EGFP-Cdc42(T17N) were positively correlated with increased OXT content in robo2+/+ (p<0.01, adj. R2 = 0.74).
source: In contrast, expression levels of EGFP-Cdc42(T17N) were positively correlated with increased OXT content in robo2+/+ (Figure 7D; p<0.01, adj. R2 = 0.74).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The positive effect of EGFP-Cdc42(T17N) on synaptic OXT content was dampened in robo2-/- mutants (p=0.35, Adj. R2 = 0.52).
source: However, the positive effect of EGFP-Cdc42(T17N) on synaptic OXT content was dampened in robo2-/- mutants (Figure 7D; p=0.35, Adj. R2 = 0.52), a finding which is consistent with the fact that Robo2 inactivation leads to increased levels of active GTP-bound Cdc42, which may counteract Cdc42(T17N).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Robo2 inactivation leads to increased levels of active GTP-bound Cdc42, which may counteract Cdc42(T17N).
source: However, the positive effect of EGFP-Cdc42(T17N) on synaptic OXT content was dampened in robo2-/- mutants (Figure 7D; p=0.35, Adj. R2 = 0.52), a finding which is consistent with the fact that Robo2 inactivation leads to increased levels of active GTP-bound Cdc42, which may counteract Cdc42(T17N).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the dampened effect of Cdc42(T17N) in robo2 mutants and knowledge of Robo2-Cdc42 signaling.

claim: Overexpression of EGFP-fused constitutively-active (i.e. GTP-bound) mutant form of CDC42, termed Cdc42(G12V), led to a dose-dependent decreased OXT levels in EGFP positive synapses similar to the low OXT levels in robo2 -/- synapses.
source: In contrast to the aforementioned effect of dominant-negative EGFP-Cdc42(T17N) mutant protein, overexpression of EGFP-fused constitutively-active (i.e. GTP-bound) mutant form of CDC42, termed Cdc42(G12V), led to a dose-dependent decreased OXT levels in EGFP positive synapses similar to the low OXT levels in robo2 -/- synapses (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The small GTPase Cdc42, which is a key regulator of actin dynamics, is in a Robo2 signaling cascade that controls the levels synaptic OXT neuropeptide.
source: These results place the small GTPase Cdc42, which is a key regulator of actin dynamics, in a Robo2 signaling cascade that controls the levels synaptic OXT neuropeptide (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of Cdc42 mutant expression experiments.

claim: Slit3-Robo2-Cdc42 signaling modulates synaptic actin dynamics to maintain steady-state levels of OXT neuropeptide readily primed to be secreted upon physiological demand.
source: Taken together, our findings reveal that Slit3-Robo2-Cdc42 signaling modulates synaptic actin dynamics to maintain steady-state levels of OXT neuropeptide readily primed to be secreted upon physiological demand.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Oxytocin is a classical evolutionarily conserved neuropeptide involved in the maintenance of various homeostatic functions.
source: Oxytocin is a classical evolutionarily conserved neuropeptide, which is involved in the maintenance of various homeostatic functions and whose major axonal release site is the posterior pituitary, also known as the neurohypophysis (Pearson and Placzek, 2013; Wircer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on oxytocin function.

claim: The major axonal release site of oxytocin is the posterior pituitary, also known as the neurohypophysis.
source: Oxytocin is a classical evolutionarily conserved neuropeptide, which is involved in the maintenance of various homeostatic functions and whose major axonal release site is the posterior pituitary, also known as the neurohypophysis (Pearson and Placzek, 2013; Wircer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on oxytocin release sites.

claim: Hypothalamic neurosecretory cells produce the neuropeptides vasopressin and oxytocin that are packed into large dense core vesicles (LDCV) and are transported along the axons that terminate in the neurohypophysis.
source: Thus, hypothalamic neurosecretory cells produce the neuropeptides vasopressin and oxytocin that are packed into large dense core vesicles (LDCV) and are transported along the axons that terminate in the neurohypophysis.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of hypothalamic neurosecretory cell function.

claim: Upon physiological demand, the neuropeptide is released into the blood stream to influence the function of target cells throughout the body.
source: Upon physiological demand, the neuropeptide is released into the blood stream to influence the function of target cells throughout the body (Burbach et al., 2001; Knobloch and Grinevich, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on neuropeptide release.

claim: In contrast to small neurotransmitters synaptic release, which mainly occurs in highly specialized membrane structures called active zones, neuropeptides, such as OXT, are released from LDCVs from any part of the neuron, including dendrites and en passant axonal synapses.
source: In contrast to small neurotransmitters synaptic release, which mainly occurs in highly specialized membrane structures called active zones, neuropeptides, such as OXT, are released from LDCVs from any part of the neuron, including dendrites and en passant axonal synapses (Chini et al., 2017; Leng et al., 2008; Leng and Ludwig, 2008; Morris and Pow, 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on neuropeptide release mechanisms.

claim: Axonal termini of hypothalamic magnocellular OXT neurons converge into the neurohypophysis, where they form numerous en passant synapses in a form of highly dense axonal varicosities, also known as axonal swellings or Herring bodies.
source: Accordingly, axonal termini of hypothalamic magnocellular OXT neurons converge into the neurohypophysis, where they form numerous en passant synapses in a form of highly dense axonal varicosities, also known as axonal swellings or Herring bodies (Tweedle et al., 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature on neurohypophyseal anatomy.

claim: Neurohypophyseal axonal swellings have been identified as bona fide synapses that store OXT-containing LDCV and release them upon physiological demand.
source: These structures have been identified as bona fide synapses that store OXT-containing LDCV and release them upon physiological demand (Miyata et al., 2001; Wittkowski and Brinkmann, 1974).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on neurohypophyseal synapse function.

claim: The mechanisms that regulate the synaptic OXT vesicles content are unknown.
source: The mechanisms that regulate the synaptic OXT vesicles content are unknown.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the manuscript addresses.

claim: F-actin, one of the major cytoskeleton elements in synapses play a key role in synapse formation.
source: F-actin, one of the major cytoskeleton elements in synapses play a key role in synapse formation (Chia et al., 2014; Ganguly et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on F-actin function in synapses.

claim: The optically transparent zebrafish larva has a few dozens of OXT neurons, which enables analysing the function of each neuron down to the single-synapse resolution in the context of a living vertebrate animal.
source: The optically transparent zebrafish larva has a few dozens of OXT neurons, which enables analysing the function of each neuron down to the single-synapse resolution in the context of a living vertebrate animal (Blechman et al., 2011; Wircer et al., 2017; Gutnick et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on zebrafish OXT neurons.

claim: Robo-Slit signaling is known to regulate synaptogenesis and actin dynamics in other CNS regions.
source: In addition to axonal guidance, Robo-Slit signaling is also known to regulate synaptogenesis and actin dynamics in other CNS regions (Blockus and Chédotal, 2016; Campbell et al., 2007; Kidd et al., 1998; Slováková et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on Robo-Slit signaling.

claim: The role of Robo-Slit3 in OXT synapse formation and function is not known.
source: However, the role of Robo-Slit3 in OXT synapse formation and function is not known.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the manuscript addresses.

claim: Previous studies have shown that Slit-Robo signaling regulates actin dynamics during neuronal migration and axonal guidance.
source: Notably, previous studies have shown that Slit-Robo signaling regulates actin dynamics during neuronal migration and axonal guidance (Kidd et al., 1998; Slováková et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature on Slit-Robo signaling.
